opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the core problems we think about. Right now the model is pretty broken: the big labs scrape everything they can, and the people who created that data get nothing. They also have no say in how it's used. Meanwhile the most valuable data, like your medical records, your financial history, or a company's internal knowledge, never makes it into these models, because nobody wants to just hand it over.

So the question is how you let people contribute private data without giving it away. I think there are a few pieces that have to come together.

The first is confidential compute. With secure enclaves and trusted execution environments on modern GPUs, you can run training or inference so that even the operator of the hardware can't see the raw data. The data goes in encrypted, the computation happens inside the enclave, and you get an attestation proving exactly what code ran on it. The contributor doesn't have to trust a company's promise. They can verify it.

The second is attribution. If you're going to pay people, you need some way to measure how much their data contributed to the model's capabilities or to a specific output. That's an open research problem. There are techniques like influence functions and data Shapley values, but they're expensive and imperfect at scale. In practice you probably start with coarser approaches. You pay for data that measurably improves performance on some benchmark or domain, or you pay per use when a fine-tuned model built on a particular dataset gets queried.

The third is the economic and ownership layer, and this is where blockchain is actually useful rather than a buzzword. You need a neutral ledger that records who contributed what, under what license, and how revenue flows back. You want it to be programmable, so that if a model earns money, a portion is automatically routed to data contributors according to rules everyone agreed to up front. And you want it not to depend on any single company staying honest or staying in business.

Put those together and you get something like a data cooperative. A group of doctors, or patients, or a set of companies in an industry pool their data into a confidential training process. They get a model that's better than any of them could build alone. They keep ownership, and they share in the upside when others use it.

There are still hard problems. Quality control matters, because once you pay for data, people will try to game it with junk or synthetic data. Privacy leakage through the model itself is another, since models can memorize, so you need things like differential privacy on top. And getting the incentives right so it's sustainable is hard too. But I think this direction is where AI has to go if we want it to be owned by and benefit the people whose data it's built on, rather than a handful of companies.

r001.rationale: The response describes contributing private data to training inside a confidential enclave, where the computation runs without the hardware operator seeing the raw data.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish permission for inference-time retrieval from permission to train on the data.

r003.rationale: It mentions paying per query for a fine-tuned model, but does not identify recorded retrieval-time use of contributed private data as a basis for compensation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the core things we're thinking about. The way I look at it is that the current paradigm is kind of broken. You have these large labs that scrape the entire internet, train a model, and the people who actually produced that data get nothing. Not just no compensation, they don't even have a say in whether it's used, or how.

So the idea with what we're building, and this is where the blockchain and crypto piece actually becomes useful rather than just a buzzword, is that you can have a system where contributions are tracked. Someone brings data, whether that's a company with proprietary datasets or an individual who has, you know, their medical records or their writing or whatever it is, and that contribution gets recorded. Then when the model is used, when inference happens and someone pays for it, a portion of that flows back to the people whose data went into it.

Now, the hard part, and I want to be honest about this, is attribution. How much did a particular piece of data actually contribute to a given output? That's an open research problem. There's work on influence functions, there's Shapley-value-style approaches, but they're expensive and imperfect. So in practice you probably start with coarser mechanisms. Maybe you compensate based on how much data you contributed and how it affected evals during training. Maybe you have data that's gated, where the model can only access it at inference time through some retrieval mechanism, and then attribution is actually straightforward because you know exactly when it was pulled in.

The private data piece specifically is interesting because that's the data that isn't already on the internet. That's where the real value is, right? Everything public has already been consumed. So if you want models that are actually better, you need to unlock data that people aren't willing to just hand over. And they're not going to hand it over to OpenAI or Google because there's no trust there and no upside. But if there's a mechanism where they keep control, where there's confidential compute or some kind of encrypted training setup so the raw data never leaves their custody, and they get paid when it's useful, that changes the incentive completely.

And I think the ownership angle matters as much as the money. If you contribute, you should have a stake in the model. Not just a one-time payment, but ongoing participation. That's the thing that makes it a user-owned AI rather than just a different billing scheme.

r001.rationale: The response describes confidential or encrypted training that keeps raw contributed data in the provider’s custody, communicating that it can be used without being exposed to others.

r002.rationale: It discusses inference-time retrieval as an option but does not state that permission for retrieval can be separate from permission to train.

r003.rationale: It says retrieval can make attribution straightforward because the system knows when private data was pulled in, and describes paying providers when inference uses their contributions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that contributing data doesn’t have to mean making it public. You could give permission for your data to be used for a particular training task, within an environment that limits access, and receive compensation for that use. So you’re providing access under certain conditions, rather than just handing over the data.

The harder question is how to value that contribution. Paying by volume alone doesn’t necessarily make sense—a small amount of unique, useful data could be more valuable than a large amount of repetitive data. You need a way to assess its usefulness, and you need credible guarantees about how it’s used. Compensation and privacy have to be designed together.

r001.rationale: It says a provider can authorize data use for a particular training task in an access-limited environment, rather than making the data public.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish permission for inference-time retrieval from permission to train on the data.

r003.rationale: It discusses compensation for usefulness and value generally, but does not identify recorded retrieval-time use as a basis for payment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting case is where you have data that you’re not willing to put out publicly, but you are willing to let somebody use it for training. How do you make that possible, and how do you get compensated for it?

You could imagine bringing the computation to the data, so the provider doesn’t have to hand over the raw information. But then you still need to understand what that contribution was worth. If ten people provide essentially the same information, that’s different from somebody contributing something unique that makes the model substantially better.

So there are really two challenges: protecting the data while making it useful, and attributing value to it. And privacy has to extend beyond where the data is stored—you also have to consider what the model might reveal after training. I would expect this to start with fairly specific use cases, where you can measure the benefit and agree on how the provider gets paid.

r001.rationale: It describes data a provider permits others to use for training without handing over the raw information.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish permission for inference-time retrieval from permission to train on the data.

r003.rationale: It discusses valuing contributions generally, but does not identify recorded retrieval-time use as a basis for compensation.
